title: HONet: Data-Efficient Learning for Exact Cover Tasks via Hypergraph Optimization
one_liner: HONet solves logic puzzles like Sudoku with far fewer training examples by baking constraint-satisfaction directly into the network's loss function.
lead: Puzzle-solving with neural networks (machine learning models that imitate the brain) normally needs thousands of examples. Logic puzzles like Sudoku have hard rules built in: each number appears once in each row, column, and box. HONet changes the game by embedding those rules directly into the network's loss function (the error signal), so the network naturally learns to prefer valid solutions.

paras: Deep learning models solve puzzles by guessing: they learn patterns from thousands of labeled Sudoku grids. The catch is they need massive piles of data, and even then they often produce invalid answers (two 5s in the same row).

Humans know the rules going in. We never need to see a thousand Sudoku boards to solve a new one. The alternative, constraint-programming solvers, can enforce the rules perfectly—but they cannot learn. They fail on puzzle variants they were never explicitly programmed for.

callout.html: Neural networks learn from examples but ignore constraints; constraint solvers enforce rules but cannot adapt to new puzzles.

steps.text: Hypergraph encoder (a network layer shaped for constraint graphs) converts the partial grid into patterns.
Deep residual layers refine the scores for each cell, learning which number belongs where.
Quadratic programming (an optimization solver built as a layer) enforces row/column/box rules.
Geometric Consistency Loss measures how far the guess sits from a valid solution.
Backpropagation (nudging network weights to shrink error) makes the network predict better next time, because the constraint signal guides each weight update toward solutions that obey the rules.

paras: HONet modifies how the network learns to score guesses. Instead of training purely from examples, it adds a differentiable constraint layer (constraint solver built into the neural network) that forces predictions toward valid solutions.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: distance to validity
hidden.name: Geometric Consistency
paras: Geometric Consistency is how far a candidate solution sits from a valid board. If all cells follow the rules, Geometric Consistency is zero (valid). If two cells in one row hold the same number, Geometric Consistency is high (invalid).

The paper estimates this by solving a small quadratic program (a mathematical optimization problem) that finds the closest valid solution and measures the gap. The network learns to produce guesses already close to valid solutions, so fewer training examples are needed.

heat.caption: Darker means farther from a valid solution; lighter means closer. True marks highlight HONet's focus.

reads.html: The network learns how close a guess is to being a real, valid Sudoku solution. The closer the guess, the faster it learns, because the network can now refine guesses that are already nearly valid instead of starting from random invalid ones.
Geometric Consistency Loss explicitly measures the distance from the network's output to the feasible polytope (the set of all valid solutions), guiding the neural network to minimize that gap.

paras: Normally a neural network is free to guess anything. Its only feedback is the loss (error) on the labeled examples. HONet adds a second signal: if your guess breaks a Sudoku rule, it is now expensive. The network learns to explore only the region of guess-space where solutions are valid.

Why this matters: with normal training, the network wastes learning on invalid guesses that happen to match an example. HONet skips that waste and focuses on the lean set of valid solutions. So fewer examples suffice to converge (reach a good answer).

The differentiable hypergraph encoder (the constraint-aware neural layer) ensures the gradient signal (the direction to nudge weights) always points toward valid solutions. The fixed-constraint quadratic programming layer (a solver turned into a neural layer) makes the constraint signal backpropagation-friendly, so every weight update respects the rules.

math.words: Total loss = prediction error plus penalty for invalid solutions, weighted by how strong the constraint pressure is.
symbols: the total error the network tries to shrink
how far the guess differs from the labeled answer
Geometric Consistency distance: how far from a valid solution
a dial: turn it up to enforce constraints harder, down to trust examples more

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Guess: a filled grid with one broken rule (two 5s in one row).
L_pred = 2.5 (two cells are wrong compared to the labeled board).
d_GC = 1.2 (moving two numbers would fix the rule violation).
If we had not included d_GC, loss = 2.5 (network may not learn the rule).
With d_GC, loss = 6.1 (network learns valid solutions are cheaper; fewer examples needed).

math.note: The more a guess breaks the rules, the higher d_GC, and the stronger the penalty, so the network learns to avoid rule-breaking guesses because they cost more error during training.

charts.title: HONet with constraints

items.html: If the rules encoded into the quadratic program do not match the actual puzzle rules, HONet learns false constraints. The network becomes fast at solving the wrong puzzle.

If lambda (the constraint weight) is too high, the network ignores the training examples and learns only generic valid boards. If lambda is too low, it ignores the rules and falls back to normal learning.
If you train HONet on 9 x 9 Sudoku but then try to solve a 16 x 16 variant with larger numbers, the hypergraph encoder may not generalize; retraining is needed.
Set lambda from a tuning set, verify the constraint set matches the puzzle class, and test on held-out examples of the same type. HONet is data-efficient within its design envelope.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal HONet on small Sudoku grids (4 x 4, using digits 1-4). Create a training set of only 20 fully solved boards. Train a normal neural network on those 20 examples and measure its accuracy on new grids. Train HONet on the same 20 examples, with the constraint layer enforcing the Sudoku rules. Measure accuracy, valid-board rate (how many outputs are valid Sudoku), and convergence speed (number of training steps to 90% accuracy).
demo.metric_eq: Data efficiency = accuracy reached with normal network at N=1000 examples, divided by accuracy reached with HONet at N=20 examples.
demo.closing: HONet should solve 4 x 4 Sudoku boards with perfect validity and high accuracy using only 20 examples, while the normal network needs orders of magnitude more to match.
